title: 12. Cloud, Containers & Deployment: SaaS (Software as a Service)

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** SaaS is a cloud service model where the provider delivers a complete, ready-to-use application over the internet, owning the infrastructure, OS, runtime, and application code, while the customer consumes it via a browser or API and pays a subscription.
Software as a Service is the highest abstraction in the cloud service stack, and it is the model most end users actually encounter. When a sales team opens Salesforce, when an engineer joins a Slack workspace, when a designer creates a Figma file, they are using SaaS — they never see a server, never patch an OS, never configure a runtime. The provider runs the entire stack: data centers, hypervisors, operating systems, databases, application code, even the user interface. The customer's responsibility begins and ends with their data and their user configuration. Salesforce, founded in 1999, is widely credited with pioneering the model; its "No Software" logo was a deliberate shot at the on-premises CRM giants of the era like Siebel. Today SaaS is the default delivery model for nearly every business application category, from CRM (Salesforce, HubSpot) to communication (Slack, Zoom, Gmail) to design (Figma, Notion) to developer tooling (GitHub, GitLab, Datadog).

The defining property of SaaS is multi-tenancy. A single running instance of the application serves many customers (tenants), and the platform isolates their data, configuration, and users invisibly. There are three classic multi-tenancy models. In the simplest, shared-database shared-schema, every tenant's rows live in the same tables with a `tenant_id` column; queries filter by `tenant_id`, and the application enforces isolation. This is the cheapest model and scales to thousands of small tenants but is the riskiest for leaks — a missed `WHERE tenant_id = ?` clause exposes data across tenants. In the second, shared-database separate-schema, each tenant gets its own schema in the same database engine; isolation is stronger and migration is easier. In the third, separate-database per tenant, each tenant gets a dedicated database (and sometimes dedicated application instances); isolation is strongest, cost is highest, and this model is used for enterprise customers with compliance requirements. Salesforce's architecture, documented in numerous papers, uses a shared database with sophisticated row-level security for the majority of customers and dedicated instances for the largest enterprises.

The second property is subscription pricing. SaaS is sold per seat (per user per month), per usage (API calls, GB stored, minutes of video), or per tier (free, pro, enterprise). This is fundamentally different from the perpetual-license model of on-premises software, where a customer paid once and used the software forever. Subscription pricing aligns the provider's incentives with continuous improvement — if the product does not get better, the customer churns. It also makes SaaS economically accessible to small businesses that could never afford a $100K perpetual license. Slack's freemium model, where teams use the product free until they hit message-history limits, is a textbook example: the free tier drives adoption, the upgrade friction is minimal, and the per-seat pricing scales naturally with team size. By 2023 Slack had over 100K paid seats on Enterprise Grid and was generating over $1B in annual revenue.

The third property is the operational invisibility. SaaS customers never see a release note about a kernel patch, never schedule a maintenance window for an OS upgrade, never worry about capacity planning for Black Friday. The provider does all of this behind the scenes, often multiple times per day. Gmail, for example, ships production changes dozens of times per week without any user-visible downtime; Figma's collaborative editing engine receives updates continuously; Salesforce runs major version upgrades three times per year on a forced schedule. This invisibility is the value proposition: the customer's engineering team can focus entirely on their own product, not on operating vendor software. The trade-off is loss of control — customers cannot choose when to upgrade, cannot stay on an old version for stability, and cannot opt out of features they dislike. When Salesforce announces a major UI change, every customer gets it whether they want it or not.

The fourth property is the API surface. Modern SaaS products expose rich REST and webhook APIs that let customers integrate the SaaS into their own workflows. Salesforce's API is so complete that many customers build their entire internal tooling on top of Salesforce data; Slack's API powers thousands of bots and integrations; GitHub's API is the foundation of CI/CD pipelines worldwide. The API is what turns a SaaS from a closed product into a platform — and most successful SaaS companies (Salesforce, Shopify, Twilio, Stripe) eventually describe themselves as platforms because the API surface area exceeds the UI surface area. Shopify's app store, with thousands of third-party apps, is a SaaS-as-platform exemplar.

The fifth property is the data residency and compliance burden. Because SaaS holds customer data, it inherits the customer's compliance obligations — GDPR for European data, HIPAA for health data, SOC 2 for security, PCI-DSS for payment data. This forces SaaS providers to support data residency (regional deployment options), audit logging, role-based access control, encryption at rest and in transit, and contractual data processing agreements. Salesforce, Slack, and Microsoft 365 all offer regional data residency options precisely because European customers cannot legally store personal data in US regions post-Schrems II. The compliance burden is significant engineering work — a SaaS targeting enterprise customers typically spends 20–30% of its engineering capacity on compliance features that do not directly add product functionality.

The trade-off summary: SaaS trades all control and customization for zero operational burden and immediate value. For commodity capabilities like email, CRM, or chat, SaaS is almost always the right choice — operating your own email server in 2024 is a sign of organizational dysfunction. For differentiating capabilities core to the business, SaaS is risky because the provider controls the roadmap, the pricing, and the data. Notion, Figma, and Linear have all faced customer pushback when changing pricing or features, illustrating the dependency risk. The disciplined approach is to use SaaS for commodity capabilities and build (or self-host) only the differentiating core, accepting the operational burden only where the business value justifies it.

### ASCII Diagram
```
+-------------------------------------------------------+
|  SaaS Provider  (e.g., Slack, Salesforce, Notion)     |

|   |   Multi-tenant Database                   |       |

|   |   | id  |tenant| data | ... | ... |        |       |
|   |   |  1  |  A   | ...  |     |     |        |       |
|   |   |  2  |  A   | ...  |     |     |        |       |
|   |   |  3  |  B   | ...  |     |     |        |       |
|   |   |  4  |  C   | ...  |     |     |        |       |
|   |   +-----+-----+-----+-----+-----+         |       |
|   |   every query: WHERE tenant_id = ?        |       |
|   +-------------------------------------------+       |
|                      |                                |
|                      v                                |
|   +-------------------------------------------+       |
|   |   Provider-managed infra (IaaS/PaaS)     |       |
|   |   OS, runtime, patching, scaling, backup  |       |
|   +-------------------------------------------+       |
|                                                       |
|   Billing: $X/seat/mo  OR  $Y per API call           |
+-------------------------------------------------------+
```

### Walkthrough
1. Each tenant (customer organization) authenticates against the SaaS via SSO or password; the request carries a tenant identifier throughout its lifecycle.
2. A single shared application codebase serves all tenants, branching behavior on `tenant_id` for configuration, feature flags, and quotas — no per-tenant code fork.
3. The multi-tenant database stores every tenant's rows in shared tables, with `tenant_id` columns and row-level security enforcing isolation; a missed filter is the most common cause of cross-tenant data leaks.
4. The provider operates the entire stack below the application — runtime, OS, infrastructure, backups — invisibly to customers, who pay a subscription and consume via browser or API.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- Raised when a query crosses tenant boundaries.
- Mimics a multi-tenant SaaS like Notion / Confluence / Coda.
- Saas_multitenancy.py - runnable mock of a SaaS multi-tenant platform.
- Models: tenant provisioning, per-tenant isolation, row-level security,
- Subscription billing, and a leak-detection guard.
- Multi-tenant CRUD with enforced isolation
- Row-level security: filter by tenant_id ALWAYS
- Return None rather than the doc, to avoid leaking existence

**Defines:** `Tenant`, `User`, `Document`, `TenantIsolationError`, `SaaSPlatform`

```python
# saas_multitenancy.py - runnable mock of a SaaS multi-tenant platform.
# Models: tenant provisioning, per-tenant isolation, row-level security,
# subscription billing, and a leak-detection guard.
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import List, Dict, Optional
import uuid, time
from datetime import datetime, timedelta

@dataclass
class Tenant:
    tenant_id: str
    name: str
    plan: str               # free, pro, enterprise
    seats: int
    created_at: datetime
    region: str             # us, eu, ap (data residency)

@dataclass
class User:
    user_id: str
    tenant_id: str
    email: str
    role: str               # admin, member, viewer

@dataclass
class Document:
    doc_id: str
    tenant_id: str          # <-- the isolation key
    owner_id: str
    title: str
    content: str
    created_at: datetime

class TenantIsolationError(Exception):
    """Raised when a query crosses tenant boundaries."""

class SaaSPlatform:
    """Mimics a multi-tenant SaaS like Notion / Confluence / Coda."""
    def __init__(self):
        self.tenants: Dict[str, Tenant] = {}
        self.users: Dict[str, User] = {}
        self.docs: Dict[str, Document] = {}
        self.billing_records: List[Dict] = []

    # --- tenant lifecycle ---
    def provision_tenant(self, name: str, plan: str, seats: int,
                         region: str = "us") -> Tenant:
        tid = "t-" + uuid.uuid4().hex[:8]
        t = Tenant(tid, name, plan, seats, datetime.utcnow(), region)
        self.tenants[tid] = t
        print(f"[provision] tenant={tid} name={name} plan={plan} region={region}")
        return t

    def add_user(self, tenant: Tenant, email: str, role: str = "member") -> User:
        uid = "u-" + uuid.uuid4().hex[:8]
        u = User(uid, tenant.tenant_id, email, role)
        self.users[uid] = u
        return u

    # --- multi-tenant CRUD with enforced isolation ---
    def create_doc(self, tenant: Tenant, owner: User,
                   title: str, content: str) -> Document:
        if owner.tenant_id != tenant.tenant_id:
            raise TenantIsolationError("owner does not belong to tenant")
        did = "d-" + uuid.uuid4().hex[:8]
        doc = Document(did, tenant.tenant_id, owner.user_id,
                       title, content, datetime.utcnow())
        self.docs[did] = doc
        return doc

    def list_docs(self, tenant: Tenant) -> List[Document]:
        # Row-level security: filter by tenant_id ALWAYS
        return [d for d in self.docs.values() if d.tenant_id == tenant.tenant_id]

    def get_doc(self, tenant: Tenant, doc_id: str) -> Document:
        doc = self.docs.get(doc_id)
        if doc is None or doc.tenant_id != tenant.tenant_id:
            # Return None rather than the doc, to avoid leaking existence
            raise TenantIsolationError(f"doc {doc_id} not accessible to tenant {tenant.tenant_id}")
        return doc

    # --- subscription billing ---
    PRICING = {"free": 0, "pro": 12, "enterprise": 35}   # $/seat/month
    def bill_tenant(self, tenant: Tenant, month: str) -> Dict:
        amount = tenant.seats * self.PRICING[tenant.plan]
        record = {"tenant": tenant.tenant_id, "month": month,
                  "seats": tenant.seats, "plan": tenant.plan,
                  "amount_usd": amount}
        self.billing_records.append(record)
        print(f"[bill] {tenant.name} ({tenant.plan}x{tenant.seats}) = ${amount}/mo")
        return record

    # --- compliance: data residency check ---
    def assert_region(self, tenant: Tenant, requested_region: str):
        if tenant.region != requested_region:
            raise TenantIsolationError(
                f"GDPR/Schrems-II: tenant {tenant.tenant_id} data must stay in {tenant.region}, "
                f"not {requested_region}")

    # --- leak detection: scan for docs accessible cross-tenant ---
    def audit_isolation(self) -> List[str]:
        leaks = []
        for tid, tenant in self.tenants.items():
            for doc in self.docs.values():
                if doc.tenant_id != tid:
                    # Simulate a buggy query that returned doc without filter
                    pass
            # Real audit: ensure no query path returns docs without tenant filter
        return leaks

if __name__ == "__main__":
    p = SaaSPlatform()

    acme = p.provision_tenant("Acme Corp", plan="pro", seats=50, region="us")
    beta = p.provision_tenant("Beta Inc", plan="enterprise", seats=200, region="eu")

    alice = p.add_user(acme, "alice@acme.com", role="admin")
    bob   = p.add_user(beta, "bob@beta.com", role="admin")

    d1 = p.create_doc(acme, alice, "Q3 roadmap", "private acme content")
    d2 = p.create_doc(beta, bob,   "M&A memo",  "private beta content")

    print(f"\nAcme sees {len(p.list_docs(acme))} doc(s)")
    print(f"Beta sees {len(p.list_docs(beta))} doc(s)")

    # Try cross-tenant access (should fail)
    try:
        p.get_doc(acme, d2.doc_id)
    except TenantIsolationError as e:
        print(f"\n[blocked] cross-tenant access denied: {e}")

    # Data residency check
    try:
        p.assert_region(beta, requested_region="us")
    except TenantIsolationError as e:
        print(f"[blocked] residency violation: {e}")

    # Monthly billing
    p.bill_tenant(acme, month="2024-05")
    p.bill_tenant(beta, month="2024-05")
```
